newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - The reality by-pass.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - The reality by-pass.

text.p: Our weekly commentator Russell Barton makes the point today that the economic debate has descended into puerile exchanges between the government and opposition, each seeking to allocate credit and blame for the good and bad in the economy.

As Barton notes (see Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup), the opposition has perhaps taken this to the extreme of claiming credit for the July rate cut but attributing the November cut to the government weakening the economy.

The public will never know the truth, which is simple: the Reserve Bank is entirely responsible for the current level of demand, and Labor is entirely responsible for the micro-economic background that the bank must work within.
Government fiscal policy affects demand, but the bank simply takes it into account as it manipulates the throttle.
The current administration has done nothing so far that could have had any effect yet on the economy.
Economic policy works with enormous lags. The tool with most immediate effect is assumed to be monetary policy, but it is not a political responsibility, and has not been for years.
Besides, this year's monetary policy can have had no effect yet, even if the government did carry the responsibility for it.
A government's input is only the macro effect of fiscal policy and the extremely vague, ambiguous and heavily lagged effect of micro-economic policy.

So, for example, Treasurer Peter Costello claims the credit for both monetary easings, but the rate cuts were driven by the Reserve Bank's view of soft price pressure next year (with the current economic flat spot undoubtedly evidence of that).

Now how can Costello claim credit for next year's inflationary pressure? He cannot, of course, except for the unproven claim that the new industrial policy will ease wage pressure. The bank, of course, makes no such assumption.
On the other hand, how can the opposition assert that the government is responsible for the current flatness in the economy?

The only action the government has taken that could conceivably affect demand is the budget, but it was announced less than three months ago and little of its fiscal tightening has yet flowed through.
Again, the current rate of economic growth is the result of former Reserve Bank Governor Bernie Fraser aiming for as much activity as he dared.

If he dared not aim for more, it was because he feared that inflation would rise -- and the sensitivity of the economy to inflation is micro-economic, which is still firmly Labor's responsibility, and will be for years.
Unemployment is perhaps the best illustration of the political debate's ability to bypass simple economic reality.
The opposition blames the government for the unemployment rate. But unemployment started rising late last year, when Labor was in power.
